summary: Adds an IMAP extension that lets a client ask the server to adapt or transcode message attachments, for example to a form that suits a small device. The client can spell out the conversion it wants, or let the server decide from what it knows about the client, the user, or the server settings. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: Suppose a friend mails you a huge photo, but your phone screen is tiny. This lets your phone ask the mail post office to shrink the photo before delivering it.

what does the imap convert capability do
subtitle: An IMAP extension that lets a client ask the server to convert attachments and headers before download.

tldr.problem: Mobile and other limited clients often cannot display or afford to download attachments in their original format, size or character set.
tldr.mechanism: CONVERT adds CONVERSIONS, CONVERT and UID CONVERT commands to IMAP. The client names a target media type and parameters, or lets the server pick, and gets the converted part back in a CONVERTED response without the stored message being changed.
tldr.outcome: Servers that advertise CONVERT and BINARY can adapt body parts and decode headers on request. Several security cautions apply, since conversion code can be attacked and cannot preserve signatures.

today: RFC 5259 is a Proposed Standard from July 2008 and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the CONVERT capability in the IANA IMAP Capability registry.

sections.title: Purpose of CONVERT
sections.content:
RFC 5259 defines the CONVERT extension to IMAP. It lets a client ask for adaptation or transcoding of attachments, either by giving the exact conversion details or by letting the server decide from what it knows about the client, user or administrator preferences, or server settings.

The extension is primarily intended to be useful to mobile clients. A server can convert body parts to formats suited to a device, and if it knows the device's characteristics it can optimize results, for example the form factor of pictures. How the server learns those characteristics is out of scope.

Conversion of attachments during streaming is out of scope and is left to a separate Lemonade WG document.
sections.plainLanguage: Your phone can ask the mail server to turn an attachment into something that suits your phone, like a smaller picture.

sections.title: Capability and Ground Rules
sections.content:
A server claiming compliance MUST support the IMAP Binary specification (RFC 3516) and MUST return both CONVERT and BINARY in its CAPABILITY response.

Conversions only affect what is sent to the client. The original data in the message store MUST NOT be altered. The RFC gives the reasons: the original stays available to other clients, replies and forwards can use the original, signatures can still be verified, and BODYSTRUCTURE information is preserved. How the server performs the conversion is not specified.
sections.plainLanguage: The post office makes a changed copy for you and leaves the original letter in the filing cabinet, so everyone else still sees the real one.

sections.title: Discovering Available Conversions
sections.content:
The CONVERSIONS command takes a source MIME type and a target MIME type, and both can be wildcards, either partial (as in text/*) or complete. It is allowed in the Authenticated and Selected states. The server answers with untagged CONVERSION responses, each naming a source type, a target type and an optional list of supported conversion parameters. If nothing matches, no CONVERSION response is returned.

For example, asking for conversions from image/gif to image/jpeg can return the parameters pix-y, pix-x and image-interleave. The parameter names come from the registry established by RFC 2506, and they are case-insensitive.
sections.plainLanguage: Before ordering, you can ask the post office, what can you turn a GIF picture into? It lists its options.

sections.title: The CONVERT and UID CONVERT Commands
sections.content:
CONVERT and UID CONVERT are modeled on FETCH and UID FETCH. The client gives a sequence set, the conversion parameters and data items, and the server replies with one untagged CONVERTED response per message. One command performs a single type of conversion, so a client needing several conversions issues several commands and MAY pipeline them. Unlike FETCH, CONVERT never sets the \Seen flag.

The data items include BINARY[...] (the converted part as binary, with the same partial semantics as FETCH), BINARY.SIZE (the converted size), BODYPARTSTRUCTURE (the MIME structure of the converted part) and AVAILABLECONVERSIONS (the target types possible). The server MUST respect the target type and parameters the client specifies.

A client can use NIL in place of a target type, called the default conversion, so the server picks a suitable type. Servers are REQUIRED to support it. Without knowledge of the device, the server should pick the most standard type in that category, such as text/plain or image/jpeg. Clients SHOULD avoid the default conversion unless they have signalled their capabilities to the server.

The command CONVERT 2 ("APPLICATION/PDF") BINARY[3] asks for body part 3 of message 2 as a PDF. A UID CONVERT MUST include the UID data item in the response, and an EXPUNGE response MUST NOT be sent during a plain CONVERT.
sections.plainLanguage: You hand the post office a slip saying which letter, which part, and what shape you want it in. They send back the changed copy. If you just say, whatever works, they choose for you.

sections.title: Conversion Parameters and Headers
sections.content:
Parameters refine a conversion. For instance PIX-X and PIX-Y give target picture dimensions, and charset sets the character set. A server MUST support charset conversions for text/plain, including from the ISO-8859 sets named in the RFC (iso-8859-1 to iso-8859-8, and iso-8859-15) to utf-8. It MUST recognize the charset parameter for text/plain, text/html, text/css, text/csv, text/enriched and text/xml.

If a character cannot be represented in the target charset, the server MUST fail the conversion with an ERROR BADPARAMETERS response, unless the client supplied the unknown-character-replacement parameter, which this RFC registers with IANA. The informative section on mobile use suggests HTML to plain text conversion and gif, jpeg and png image conversion with size, width, height and resize options.

Header conversion uses BODY[HEADER], BODY[section.HEADER] and BODY[section.MIME] with the default conversion and a required CHARSET parameter. The server MUST decode RFC 2047 encoded words and re-encode them in that charset, leaves undecodable words as they are, and SHOULD also handle RFC 2231 parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: You can add instructions such as make the picture this wide, or write it in this alphabet. If it cannot be done without losing letters, the post office says so instead of guessing, unless you gave it a stand-in symbol.

sections.title: Sizes, Failures and Limits
sections.content:
BINARY.SIZE MUST return an exact value that does not change during the IMAP session, so a client can download in chunks. Clients MUST NOT cache converted sizes beyond a session or assume a later session gives the same result, because server transcoders might be upgraded. The RFC warns the request can be expensive, since the server often must do the conversion first.

A syntactically invalid media type SHOULD give a tagged BAD, and an unrecognized one gives NO. Failures are reported with an ERROR phrase in the CONVERTED response, with codes TEMPFAIL, BADPARAMETERS and MISSINGPARAMETERS. Tagged NO response codes include TEMPFAIL, MAXCONVERTMESSAGES and MAXCONVERTPARTS, which let a server refuse requests naming too many messages or parts. If at least one conversion succeeds, the server MUST return OK.

Servers SHOULD cache converted parts for performance, should limit the number cached to resist denial of service, and SHOULD be able to cache at least 2 conversions at a time.
sections.plainLanguage: The post office tells you exactly how big the changed copy is, and if it cannot make it, it tells you why and whether to try again later. It may also say one request is too big.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Conversions can be risky: they might yield a damaging executable, exploit a buffer overflow in a media codec or parser, or enable denial of service, for example by requesting an image scaled to extremely large dimensions. Servers SHOULD refuse CPU-expensive conversions, avoid dangerous ones and verify results where possible. Clients SHOULD use mutual SASL authentication and the SASL/TLS integrity layer.

A client cannot verify the authenticity of a server-converted signed part such as one inside multipart/signed. A client that does not trust the server can download the signed object, verify it and convert it itself.

A client could also APPEND a crafted bad message and then CONVERT it to attack the server. Servers SHOULD log the client's authentication identity on APPEND and CONVERT, and SHOULD isolate the conversion library from the privileged mailstore, perhaps in a distinct process.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing files can be dangerous if a file is booby-trapped, so the post office should do the work in a separate, locked room and keep a record of who asked.

items.label: Temporary failure
items.desc: The request failed for now; the client MAY retry. In an ERROR phrase it carries a wait time in minutes.

items.label: Too many messages
items.desc: Server will convert at most the given number of messages per command.

items.label: Too many parts
items.desc: Server will convert at most the given number of body parts of a message at once.

items.label: Parameters not usable
items.desc: ERROR phrase: parameters not understood, invalid or not honorable; lists them.

items.label: Parameters required
items.desc: ERROR phrase: parameters required for this conversion were not in the request.
